Lines of credit and HELOCs float at prime plus a margin; a higher rate raises payments and lowers borrowing
Gross & Souleles (2002a); Brigden, Chrystal & Mizen (2000); Attanasio, Goldberg & Kyriazidou (2008)
Credit-card rates barely move with prime: the effect works through lines of credit and HELOCs
Higher unemployment raises income risk, defaults and write-offs, and makes lenders tighten
Brigden, Chrystal & Mizen (2000) find a small positive short-run effect (borrowing to smooth spending): the negative effect builds over time
Consumer credit finances durable goods and spending; spending above its long-run level is partly borrowed
Bacchetta & Gerlach (1997); Ludvigson (1999); Brigden, Chrystal & Mizen (2000)
Moves at the same time as credit: lag it or use it as a check rather than a driver
Retail purchases, especially durables, are often paid with credit cards and lines of credit
Car purchases are largely financed with auto loans; sales drive new loan origination
Relevant if auto loans are part of the personal loan balance
Confident households spend more on durables and borrow more to do it
Carroll, Fuhrer & Wilcox (1994); Brigden, Chrystal & Mizen (2000)
Tightening raises the cost of variable-rate personal credit and lowers household loan demand
den Haan, Sumner & Yamashiro (2007); Ciccarelli, Maddaloni & Peydró (2015)

Easier lending standards, higher limits and lower down-payments raise borrowing; households borrow much of any extra credit offered
Fernández-Corugedo & Muellbauer (2006); Lown & Morgan (2006); Agarwal et al. (2018); Gross & Souleles (2002a)
Map to the Bank of Canada Senior Loan Officer Survey (household lending conditions) or a credit conditions index
More insolvencies mean write-offs and tighter lending to riskier borrowers
Rising delinquency leads lenders to cut limits and tighten approval
Highly indebted households cut new borrowing and spending when conditions turn
Left out by default: the ratio contains the loans being forecast, so it is not a genuine driver
Higher prices raise nominal spending to finance, but erode real incomes and bring tighter policy
Brigden, Chrystal & Mizen (2000) find a negative effect on unsecured lending in the UK
